Limited exposure can contribute to heightened anxiety, decreased familiarity with pediatric anatomy and physiology, and reduced preparedness for management of pediatric emergencies, especially in high-acuity and time-sensitive situations. Methods We developed a pediatric anesthesia refresher curriculum delivered as a three-hour, simulation-based workshop during the pediatric anesthesia rotation at a children’s hospital over a twelve-month period. It focused on common perioperative pediatric anesthesia emergencies alongside hands-on practice of airway management and vascular access. Participants were surveyed to assess perceived preparedness, confidence, and anxiety regarding pediatric anesthesia care. title: Exploring Students' Perspectives on Using Al Tools to Improve an Interprofessional Education [IPE] Patient Safety Course Across Health Professions Education Programs
text_snippet: Exploring Students' Perspectives on Using Al Tools to Improve an Interprofessional Education [IPE] Patient Safety Course Across Health Professions Education Programs This quantitative cross-sectional study evaluated the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) tools in an Interprofessional Education (IPE) Patient Safety course among clinical-year undergraduate students (Medicine, Nursing, Pharmacy; N = 312) at a health sciences college in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia. Data collected via four validated instruments (SCEQ, Inter-professional Course Evaluation Scale, H-PEPSS, and TAM) demonstrated high baseline AI Acceptance ( M = 4.52 ± 0.72) and perceived Patient Safety Competency ( M = 4.47 ± 0.75). Female students exhibited significantly higher safety competency ( p = 0.021) and AI acceptance ( p = 0.047). Higher academic performance (GPA 4.50–5.0) and older age (≥ 24 years) were significantly associated with greater engagement and competency ( p R2 = 0.764, p p 0.001), followed by IPE Course Evaluation (β = 0.307, p 0.001) and Student Engagement (β = 0.143, p = 0.002). Strategic AI integration within team-based learning enhances perceived patient safety competencies across health professions. title: Emotional Empathy and Emotional Empathy Training for Medical Students: A Systematic Review
text_snippet: Emotional Empathy and Emotional Empathy Training for Medical Students: A Systematic Review Introduction Emotional empathy is a key component of medical professionalism, enhancing doctor–patient communication, trust, treatment adherence, and clinical outcomes. However, research suggests that emotional empathy tends to decline during medical education, with potential negative impacts on both patient care and student well-being. Objective This systematic review explores how emotional empathy in medical students is influenced by educational interventions integrated into the medical curriculum. Methods A systematic search of PubMed and Web of Science was conducted in January 2025, following PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Out of 139 articles, eight studies met the inclusion criteria. Due to heterogeneity in design and outcomes, a narrative synthesis was performed. Results All included studies reported some effect of educational interventions on emotional empathy although impacts varied across subdimensions. Reflective sessions, communication training, and improvisation-based learning appeared particularly beneficial. title: Collective Educator Efficacy in Medical Education: A Conceptual Synthesis and Framework for Program Evaluation
text_snippet: Collective Educator Efficacy in Medical Education: A Conceptual Synthesis and Framework for Program Evaluation Introduction Program evaluation in medical education often emphasizes outcomes such as examination performance, competency attainment and learner satisfaction, but these indicators do not fully explain why programs with similar structures can produce different educational results. This review introduces collective educator efficacy as a potentially important but underexamined determinant of program implementation and program quality. Methods We conducted a structured narrative review with conceptual synthesis, drawing literature from medical education, collective efficacy research, organizational psychology, faculty development and program evaluation. The review used transparent search and selection procedures and was guided by published standards for high-quality narrative reviews. Results The literature suggests that educational outcomes are shaped not only by curriculum design, but also by faculty coordination, shared expectations, psychological safety, assessment calibration and the collective capacity to implement, adapt and sustain educational practices. title: The Dual-Identity Dilemma: A Comparative Study of Mentorship Structural Barriers in Military and Civilian Medical Education
text_snippet: The Dual-Identity Dilemma: A Comparative Study of Mentorship Structural Barriers in Military and Civilian Medical Education Introduction Mentorship functions as a stabilizing relational framework in high-demand medical education environments. This international collaborative study between the Defence Services Medical Academy (DSMA) and Avalon University School of Medicine (AUSOM) examines the “Dual-Identity Dilemma”—the structural tension between professional medical identity and institutional military role expectations. While mentorship is central to professional development, hierarchical military structures may shape its psychosocial accessibility. Methods An explanatory sequential mixed-methods design (QUAN→QUAL) was conducted. Quantitative survey data were collected from 251 DSMA cadets and 100 AUSOM students to provide a civilian international benchmark. Within DSMA, qualitative interviews (n = 8 mentors) and focus groups (n = 8 mentees) explored identified quantitative “friction points.” Descriptive statistics, ANOVA with Bonferroni correction, and effect size reporting (partial η 2 ) were applied. title: Implementing adult learning theories in the integration of enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS) in the continuous medical education of surgery residents
text_snippet: Implementing adult learning theories in the integration of enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS) in the continuous medical education of surgery residents Despite the recognition of Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS) principles, the implementation and adherence to the protocol remain under-discussed. This could be attributed to its inadequate integration into surgical education programs where challenges and limitations are evident. This study aims to initiate an adult learning cycle for surgical residents and measure the impact of a multifaceted approach in integrating a new program into continuous health professions’ education. This study adopts a cross-sectional multicentric approach. The methodology involves three main steps: firstly, administering a pre-assessment form to challenge students’ existing knowledge and initiate the adult learning model; secondly, raising awareness and sharing educational resources; and finally, distributing a post-assessment form to assess the consolidation of the relayed information. Statistical analysis revealed a significant improvement in the scores of digestive surgery residents after receiving educational resources. title: The REASON Framework for quality-assured MCQ assessment in health-professional and bioscience education: six practical steps from question design to post-assessment analysis
text_snippet: The REASON Framework for quality-assured MCQ assessment in health-professional and bioscience education: six practical steps from question design to post-assessment analysis Multiple-choice question (MCQ) assessment is widely used across health-professional and bioscience education because it enables broad curriculum sampling, efficient administration, objective scoring and post-assessment review of item performance. However, MCQ assessment quality is not guaranteed by the format alone. It depends on how items are designed, reviewed, administered, analysed and used within the wider assessment system. This narrative review synthesises practical principles for quality-assured and inclusive MCQ assessment in health-professional and bioscience education. It considers how question design, pre-assessment review and post-assessment analysis can support assessment decisions that are valid, reliable, fair and well-evidenced. The review synthesises literature relating to item writing, distractor quality, blueprinting, peer review, faculty development in the form of item-writer training, accessibility, feedback, post-test item analysis, reliability, validity and standard setting, and organises it around three assessment-lifecycle pillars: question design, pre-assessment review and post-assessment analysis. title: Sex and Gender Representation in Cardiothoracic Surgical Textbooks
text_snippet: Sex and Gender Representation in Cardiothoracic Surgical Textbooks Objective Gender differences among disease patterns have been well-established across many diseases and procedures. However, female patients have consistently experienced poorer healthcare outcomes. This is particularly prominent among heart and lung diseases, which represent two leading causes of mortality internationally. To address this, female healthcare outcomes need to be investigated, and solutions placed at the forefront of healthcare advancement, beginning with medical education. The aim of this study was to evaluate sex and gender representation in cardiothoracic surgical textbooks used by medical schools within the Republic and Northern Ireland. Design and setting Public online databases of medical libraries within the Republic and Northern Ireland were searched using the term ‘cardiothoracic’ and resulting texts were screened for relevancy. Sex and gender representation was evaluated in each chosen text using a modified version of the validated protocol outlined by Alexanderson. 20 This involved evaluation of epidemiological data, risk factors, disease presentation, treatment guidelines and post-operative outcomes, as well as illustrations and radiographic images. title: Outcomes of a Multi-campus, Multi-semester Applied Critical Care Research Elective
text_snippet: Outcomes of a Multi-campus, Multi-semester Applied Critical Care Research Elective Objective The Research in Critical Care Pharmacotherapy elective implemented a novel approach that promoted collaborative research across four campuses for up to four semesters of credit. Methods Retrospective evaluation over five years of a multi-campus, multi-semester research elective course in a traditional Doctor of Pharmacy program. title: 10 insights for harnessing artificial intelligence in scientific research: supervisor perspectives
text_snippet: 10 insights for harnessing artificial intelligence in scientific research: supervisor perspectives Background Artificial intelligence (AI) transforms scientific research and publication by supporting all aspects of research from setting up hypothesis and research objectives to data analysis and manuscript preparation. Its widespread use in postgraduate research by students improves efficiency and feedback, but also raises concerns related to academic integrity, ethical behavior, algorithmic bias, hallucinated outputs, copyright issues, and mainly, preservation of students’ critical thinking skills. This article presents supervisor-oriented guidance for the responsible integration of AI into scientific research supervision. Methods We have undertaken narrative synthesis based on published manuscripts as well as our collective supervisory experience with AI-assisted research projects. Published literature evidence and practical experience were integrated to develop 10 insights for supervisors guiding research students who use AI tools during all aspects of their research. title: The Wellbeing Tri-Hazard: an evidence-informed model for medical student wellbeing
text_snippet: The Wellbeing Tri-Hazard: an evidence-informed model for medical student wellbeing Wellbeing is a central concern in medical education, yet the term remains inconsistently defined and difficult for educators to measure, let alone meaningfully remediate. Although many wellbeing initiatives focus on specific interventions—such as resiliency training, mindfulness, or support services—these approaches often fail to explain how wellbeing becomes destabilized during the realities of medical training. This Opinion Article introduces the Wellbeing Tri-Hazard model as an evidence-informed conceptual framework for scholarly discussion. The model is grounded in previously published literature on wellbeing, resiliency, medical education, student support, and systems-level influences. I define wellbeing as an ecosystem underpinned by cognitive, physical, and institutional components. Wellbeing is achieved when this tri-dimensional relationship is in balance, creating a positive impact on mental and physical health, which promotes motivation, self-regulation and resiliency. title: From Theory to Impact: Outcomes from a Learning Theory-Driven Pilot Premedical Pathway Program
text_snippet: From Theory to Impact: Outcomes from a Learning Theory-Driven Pilot Premedical Pathway Program Background/Introduction Premedical pathway programs serve as a vehicle to advance equity and access for students who have experienced systemic barriers to education, yet few programs explicitly address the academic competency development necessary for success in rigorous science courses. Undergraduate premedical students face significant cognitive load, and success requires both content knowledge and metacognitive learning strategies (MLS) needed to process, integrate, and retrieve information. Methods This pilot study examined whether a learning-theory-driven summer intensive grounded in self-regulated learning (SRL) and delivered by a trained learning specialist produced significant gains in students’ skill and motivation. A pre-post design was employed with 16 students in the Program. The Learning and Study Strategies Inventory (LASSI) was administered at program entry and exit; a qualitative survey was analyzed using deductive thematic coding. title: Identifying Mental Health Risk in Medical Students: A Quantitative Analysis of Wellness Assessments for First- and Third-Year Students at the University of Ottawa
text_snippet: Identifying Mental Health Risk in Medical Students: A Quantitative Analysis of Wellness Assessments for First- and Third-Year Students at the University of Ottawa Introduction An alarming prevalence of burnout among medical students has been reported in many countries, including Canada. To design resilience and wellness programs, it is important to explore individual risk factors. This article presents an example of a Wellness Assessment Program for medical students at the University of Ottawa. The goal was to identify risk factors for poorer mental health outcomes among medical students at the University of Ottawa. Methods We conducted a quantitative study using a Wellness Assessment Questionnaire among four cohorts of first- and third-year students. Results Risk factors that significantly impacted the mental health of 1 st and 3 rd year medical students at the University of Ottawa were physical health, sleep/fatigue, social support, education and career, stress, and drug and/or alcohol use. title: “An Even Playing Field”: Non-Clinical Simulation for Leadership Development Among Pediatric Interns
text_snippet: “An Even Playing Field”: Non-Clinical Simulation for Leadership Development Among Pediatric Interns Background Graduate training programs are tasked with preparing trainees to lead clinical teams. Currently, there is little consensus on how to develop their interpersonal leadership skills, and pediatric programs tend to focus on senior residents. Targeting pediatric interns with strategies for developing interpersonal leadership skills provides more opportunity to consolidate and apply these skills during training. Objective We aimed to understand how simulation, informed by cognitive load theory and psychological safety, facilitates the development of interpersonal leadership skills among pediatric interns. Methods Pediatric interns participated in an outdoor wilderness simulation repeated 4 times between July–November 2022. The simulation and debrief focused on consensus decision-making and communication. To explore if and how simulation outside of clinical teams and devoid of clinical content fostered interpersonal leadership skills, we conducted semi-structured focus groups after each debrief. title: From Receiving to Giving: A Scoping Review on Teaching and Assessing Residents as Feedback Providers
text_snippet: From Receiving to Giving: A Scoping Review on Teaching and Assessing Residents as Feedback Providers Background Feedback is a cornerstone of medical education. Although residents are routinely expected to provide feedback to junior learners, this skill is often neglected as a competency in postgraduate medical education programs. To our knowledge, there have been no scoping reviews on how residents are taught or assessed to provide feedback. Methods Following the Arksey and O’Malley framework, we performed a database search (MEDLINE, Embase, PsycInfo, Web of Science) from inception to October 2025. Title-abstract and full-text screening were completed in duplicate, after training on inclusion and exclusion criteria. Data extraction included year, country, program, level, and narrative information on the teaching and assessment of resident-provided feedback. Analysis included descriptive statistics and an iterative process of theme development. Results After 2518 duplicates were removed, 8613 studies underwent abstract-title screening, 89 underwent full-text screening, and 68 were included in the review. title: Practical Tips to Improve the Medical Student Learning Experience while on the Emergency Medicine Clerkship
text_snippet: Practical Tips to Improve the Medical Student Learning Experience while on the Emergency Medicine Clerkship The emergency medicine (EM) clerkship can be a uniquely challenging clinical learning environment for students as they transition from the pre-clinical to the clinical phase of their undergraduate medical education. Despite the complexity of this transition, limited guidance exists for educators on how to best support medical students stepping into the emergency department learning environment for the very first time. Drawing on prior research from our study team and existing literature, we identify actionable tips for EM clerkship leadership and faculty. We provide the readership with 11 practical tips. These tips span pre-clinical preparation, clerkship structure, and ED-specific clinical skills to support learners. These tips aim to improve both medical student education and the medical student experience while on their EM medicine clerkship.

title: Medical Student Burnout: Underlying Causes and Solutions
text_snippet: Medical Student Burnout: Underlying Causes and Solutions Background The medical profession is one of the leading fields in worker and student burnout, suicide, and depression. Medical student burnout, as a subset, has been understudied; therefore, the goal of this project is to study medical student burnout and propose solutions. Methods A survey comprising 15 questions that inquired about current burnout, views on a decompressed curriculum, and burnout mitigation strategies was sent to 58 students at the institution where this study was conducted. Interviews were conducted with 15 participants to further elaborate on burnout. Results This study found that ~48.0% of respondents reported they were experiencing burnout. Second-year medical students exhibited the highest level of burnout. Only 37.3% of the students claimed that STEP 1 going pass/fail helped alleviate the impending stress of residency applications, while 81.0% of the students found that the decompressed curriculum helped attenuate burnout. Conclusion STEP 1 grading was amended to Pass/Fail for wellness per AAMC. At our institution, STEP 1 is taken at the end of the second year, yet second-year students are the most burnt out. title: "Teaching at the Crossroads" How educators can navigate ethical dilemmas in training : practical tips
text_snippet: "Teaching at the Crossroads" How educators can navigate ethical dilemmas in training : practical tips Background When medical trainees enter the clinical setting, they find themselves in a perplexing position where they have to care for patients, acquire medical knowledge, strengthen clinical skills, adhere to the hierarchy of healthcare teams, and obtain positive assessments. Balancing these competing objectives while trying to preserve individual integrity can be a source of ethical dilemmas. Ethical dilemmas are acknowledged as problematic situations in which learners witness or participate in a behavior that they deem improper, wrong, unethical, or against their values. Remarkably, despite the imperative need to address the aforementioned issues, a code of silence has long prevailed among trainees and educators regarding these challenges. Recently, there has been growing recognition among medical educators of the distinct ethical dilemmas inherent to medical trainees’ status in clinical settings, prompting efforts to explore their underlying roots and consequences. Methods The authors acknowledge and respond to the need for clear guidance in understanding the theoretical foundation relevant to these ethical conundrums and how to address them. title: Reimagining Coaching in Generative AI: Theory-Informed Feedback Co-Design
text_snippet: Reimagining Coaching in Generative AI: Theory-Informed Feedback Co-Design Context Educators struggle to prototype feedback design for coaching in Generative AI (GenAI) learning environment. Feedback supports healthcare professionals (HCPs) to keep pace with evolving knowledge, skills, and professional practice. Designing feedback for GenAI learning environments may offload the coaching resource delivery challenges. Current approaches to design often fall short of addressing the diverse patients/caregivers (P/Cs)’ perspectives, learner readiness levels, and workplace realities of HCPs. This limits its responsiveness to societal health needs. Approach This paper adopted an Educational Design Research (EDR) approach to prototype GenAI learning environment and establish a feedback design with principles of (1) experiential learning space; (2) social cultural learning context; (3) reflective learning mechanism. Outcomes This context-sensitive design in GenAI learning environment connect to three overarching concerns: questionable acceptability of non-human coaching feedback, developmental limitation in the linear pathway of research and technology, and inclusivity of P/Cs′ voices. title: The GEMstone Maze – an interactive and immersive clinical skills and data interpretation game for medical students at Swansea university.
text_snippet: The GEMstone Maze – an interactive and immersive clinical skills and data interpretation game for medical students at Swansea university. Background The use of gamified and interactive resources in medical education has experienced a boon due to the need for remote learning during the COVID-19 pandemic. The GEMstone Maze was developed in 2024 to provide an evidence-based, engaging, immersive, and motivating educational resource for Swansea University medical students with a realistic set of challenges mirroring clinical practice and exams. Methods 105 Swansea University Year 2 medical students, split into small teams, completed a 90-minute, four-zone interactive immersive game projected onto the walls of the immersive simulation rooms. The games were based on clinical data interpretation, diagnostic skills, clinical examination skills, procedural skills, and Multiple-Choice Questions (MCQs). A two-way mixed ANOVA was used to compare students who had the GEMstone Maze before their clinical data exam (intervention group) with previous year 2 students who did not have the intervention (control group). Within-group comparisons between pre- and post-maze clinical data examinations for both groups were also analysed. title: Anatomy Outreach as a Context for Professional Identity Development in Medical Students
text_snippet: Anatomy Outreach as a Context for Professional Identity Development in Medical Students Purpose/Background Building Lasting Anatomical Skills Together (BLAST) is a student-led outreach program at our institution that introduces high school students to anatomy through medical student-led sessions. This study describes BLAST as an educational and community engagement initiative and explores how participation provides a context for professional identity formation (PIF) among medical students. Methods Survey data, including both quantitative responses and qualitative reflections, were collected from 30 medical students (M1-M4) who participated in BLAST. Qualitative responses were used to examine patterns and to identify themes related to professional identity development. Results Participation was highest during the preclerkship years, particularly among first-year medical students. Involvement in BLAST was associated with the development of communication and teaching skills, increased confidence, and opportunities for leadership and mentorship. title: Handling handoffs: a national survey of program directors on standardized handoffs in emergency medicine training
text_snippet: Handling handoffs: a national survey of program directors on standardized handoffs in emergency medicine training Background Structured handoffs in Emergency Medicine (EM) are known to improve patient care, and several prior studies have proposed specific processes. However, little is known regarding current implementation and education of trainees on structured handoffs in EM residency programs. Methods We surveyed EM program directors (PDs) using a mixed-methods approach to explore the current use of and education regarding structured handoffs in residency programs. Descriptive data were reported as percentages. An adjunct analysis of free-text responses was done using the framework method. Results A total of 174 PD responses were collected for a response rate of 63%. Of those, 69% (119/172) currently use a structured handoff, though among those who answered the frequency question (n = 103), only about half (51%) report its use as “very often,” suggesting consistent use in approximately one-third of responding programs. title: A Thousand Papercuts: Email Communication Difficulties and their Impact on Faculty Well-being
text_snippet: A Thousand Papercuts: Email Communication Difficulties and their Impact on Faculty Well-being Background Burnout and well-being among academic faculty have garnered substantial attention within the medical education literature. While various contributors to burnout have been studied, the role of email management remains relatively unexplored. Objective This study investigated the impact of email challenges on faculty well-being using the Job Demands-Resources model as a framework. Methods In 2023 the authors surveyed faculty across accredited medical education institutions to assess experiences with email management. They collected data on email communication difficulties and their impact on faculty well-being. Results Respondents included 447 faculty from 115 institutions. Results indicated that faculty spent large amounts of time on email-related tasks, and that the demands of email management are exacerbated by institutional firewalls, managing multiple professional email accounts, frequent required password changes, automatic deletion or archiving of emails, and other technical issues. title: Grounded Yet Ascending: Faculty Development in a Time of Reduced Budgets and Travel
text_snippet: Grounded Yet Ascending: Faculty Development in a Time of Reduced Budgets and Travel Introduction Recent federal funding cuts have created pauses in admissions, hiring, and execution of research studies at academic medical centers internationally. These monetary reductions have also impacted allowances for non-essential faculty travel. As a result, faculty may now be faced with challenges in how they obtain professional development. Methods A cross-sectional, exploratory study was implemented to discover the impact of funding cuts on faculty travel for professional development opportunities, as well as strategies medical educators are using to mitigate the current landscape. Results Findings indicate that faculty now must use alternative methods to obtain professional development and that institutional guidance is lacking in how to do so. Discussion Authors provide concrete action steps for faculty to take amidst this challenge to remain engaged in professional development.

title: Meducide - Towards a new conceptual framework for the destruction of medical education in armed conflicts
text_snippet: Meducide - Towards a new conceptual framework for the destruction of medical education in armed conflicts Wars and armed conflicts are widely recognised as a threat to health systems, yet the destruction of medical education is still too often treated as a secondary educational disruption. This opinion article argues that attacks on medical schools, teaching hospitals, clinical placements, accreditation systems and faculty pipelines should be understood as a distinct form of long-term public health harm. I propose the term "meducide" to describe the systematic destruction, dismantling or incapacitation of medical education during war, whether by direct attack or by structural conditions that render medical training impossible. The concept builds on existing scholarship on attacks on education, structural violence and health workforce fragility, while highlighting what is distinctive about medical education. It captures not only the destruction of medical schools and teaching hospitals but also the broader erosion of the conditions necessary to train future healthcare. Therefore, it sits at the intersection of higher education, health service delivery, professional regulation and the future health workforce. title: Resident Expectations, Program Alignment, and Program Director Longevity in Obstetrics and Gynecology Residency Programs
text_snippet: Resident Expectations, Program Alignment, and Program Director Longevity in Obstetrics and Gynecology Residency Programs Introduction Residency Program Director (PD) longevity has decreased over time, 1 with many specialties citing tenure in this leadership role of 5 years or less. Burnout, lack of support, and challenges with work/life balance may be causal factors. Our aim was to examine the current tenure of PDs in this field and identify factors supportive of longevity versus challenges that may contribute to turn-over. Methods We conducted a survey-based cross-sectional study of current and former OBGYN PDs between December 2024 and March 2025. The electronic survey included demographics, questions on overall satisfaction in the role, factors lending support, and those posing challenges. Descriptive analyses summarized participant characteristics and key findings. The primary outcome analyzed was certainty of remaining in the PD role for the next five years. Associations with increasing certainty of retention were examined using ordinal logistic regression with a proportional-odds model and logit link. title: Applied insights for using Generative Artificial Intelligence in Faculty Development in Health Professions Education
text_snippet: Applied insights for using Generative Artificial Intelligence in Faculty Development in Health Professions Education Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has rapidly become accessible to health professions educators and learners, creating both opportunities and new responsibilities for faculty development (FD). GenAI can help draft, adapt, and translate educational materials, and can assist faculty developers as a “co-developer.” However, GenAI outputs require human oversight, and FD leaders must actively manage accuracy, privacy/confidentiality, equity/fairness, and sustainability concerns. This article offers a perspective on how GenAI can be leveraged as a co-developer in FD by drawing on emerging literature and discussion points from a workshop at the 8th International Faculty Development Conference in the Health Professions . Applied insights We provide eight applied insights, organised across key phases of FD work (planning, content creation, delivery, and evaluation). A standardized survey questionnaire assessed perceptions of content, organization, overall satisfaction, and likelihood to recommend. Quantitative and qualitative analysis were performed. title: Academic Stressors and Sociodemographic Vulnerabilities Among Medical Students at the University of Ottawa
text_snippet: Academic Stressors and Sociodemographic Vulnerabilities Among Medical Students at the University of Ottawa Introduction Medical students experience high levels of stress that impact their health and academic performance. Yet, to our knowledge, no prior Canadian study has explored medical training-related stressors, using a validated tool such as the Medical Student Stress Questionnaire, leaving a gap in the national literature. The objective of this study was to determine the major academic stressors and their relationship with sociodemographic factors among medical students at the University of Ottawa. Methods This cross-sectional study was conducted using a SurveyMonkey questionnaire from May to August 2024 with the 40 items of the Medical Student Stress Questionnaire. Variables were age, year of study, gender, LGBTQ2S+, ethnicity, rural/urban, living situation, financial situation, disability, and dependents. Descriptive statistics, t-tests, ANOVAs, and multiple regression analyses were conducted using SPSS v30.0. The study was approved by the University of Ottawa Research Ethics Board. Results 70 medical students participated, but 60 complete responses were analyzed (85.7%). The mean total Medical Student Stress Questionnaire score was 2.63 ± 0.79, i.e. moderate stress. title: Astonishment as a Trigger for Reflective Learning in Health Professions Education: A Focused Mapping Review with Patient Safety Implications
text_snippet: Astonishment as a Trigger for Reflective Learning in Health Professions Education: A Focused Mapping Review with Patient Safety Implications Background Experiences that interrupt routine perception—labelled in health professions education (HPE) as surprise , cognitive dissonance , unsettling encounters or wonder —are used to stimulate reflection but remain conceptually dispersed. This review examines how such experiences, treated analytically as astonishment-related triggers , are described, theorised and mobilised in HPE, and how they relate to dimensions relevant to patient safety. Methods A Focused Mapping Review and Synthesis (FMRS) was conducted. Searches were undertaken in MEDLINE, CINAHL, ERIC, PsycINFO and Google Scholar. Eligible publications were those describing educational or clinical experiences in HPE characterised by perceptual or interpretive interruption. Twelve empirical, conceptual and descriptive studies met the inclusion criteria. Data were mapped according to terminology, context, trigger type, reflective processes and safety relevance, and analysed using an interpretive synthesis approach. No formal risk of bias or certainty-of-evidence assessment was undertaken. title: The Dual-Identity Dilemma: A Comparative Study of Mentorship Structural Barriers in Military and Civilian Medical Education
text_snippet: The Dual-Identity Dilemma: A Comparative Study of Mentorship Structural Barriers in Military and Civilian Medical Education Introduction Mentorship functions as a stabilizing relational framework in high-demand medical education environments. This international collaborative study between the Defence Services Medical Academy (DSMA) and Avalon University School of Medicine (AUSOM) examines the “Dual-Identity Dilemma”—the structural tension between professional medical identity and institutional military role expectations. While mentorship is central to professional development, hierarchical military structures may shape its psychosocial accessibility. Methods An explanatory sequential mixed-methods design (QUAN→QUAL) was conducted. Quantitative survey data were collected from 251 DSMA cadets and 100 AUSOM students to provide a civilian international benchmark. Within DSMA, qualitative interviews (n = 8 mentors) and focus groups (n = 8 mentees) explored identified quantitative “friction points.” Descriptive statistics, ANOVA with Bonferroni correction, and effect size reporting (partial η 2 ) were applied. Results Mentorship expectations were high across both cohorts. However, DSMA cadets reported higher communication barriers (65.2%) compared with the civilian benchmark. title: Evaluating Clinical Reasoning in Prescribing: A Systematic Review of Assessment Tools and Approaches in Medical Education and Training
text_snippet: Evaluating Clinical Reasoning in Prescribing: A Systematic Review of Assessment Tools and Approaches in Medical Education and Training Introduction Clinical reasoning is a critical component of prescribing competency. As medical education transitioned to competency-based frameworks and digitalisation of learning and assessment, there is an urgent need to evaluate tools capable of assessing clinical reasoning in prescribing. This systematic review aimed to identify and explore assessment tools for clinical reasoning, with a focus on their effectiveness, digital adaptability, and application to prescribing clinical reasoning. Methods A comprehensive search of six databases was conducted using PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Studies were screened for inclusion based on a set of predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria, and the quality of the included ones was assessed using the MERSQI instrument. Results A total of 101 studies were included, identifying 61 assessment tools. They were categorised as written indirect assessment (62.3%) or performance-based direct assessment (37.7%). Script Concordance Tests (SCTs) and Objective Structured Clinical Examinations (OSCEs) were the most frequently used tools. title: Being a final year medicine resitter , it’s not as bad as you think- a qualitative study exploring the identity of medical students resitting final year.
text_snippet: Being a final year medicine resitter , it’s not as bad as you think- a qualitative study exploring the identity of medical students resitting final year. Background In most institutions, a relatively static proportion of students fail the final medical degree programme each year. The majority are successful at resit, so they proceed to postgraduate training. Schools vary when students sit on the final examination and whether they must resit the whole year. The Medical Licensing Assessment shapes medical school approaches. Little is known about the implications of first-time failures on students’ experience of repeating their final years. Identity theory provides a means to explore this phenomenon. Summary of methods A modified grounded theory approach was used to explore how failing medical finals affected the students and foundation-year doctors. Eighteen qualitative interviews were completed with students who had failed finals, were repeating their final year, or who were F1s having previously failed. Interviews were conducted at three time points. Summary of results Qualitative analysis highlighted that participants who fail finals described a ‘resitter identity’ which results in a different approach to clinical learning, provided an enhanced status within their new cohort, and led to personal and professional development. title: Integration of Social Science and Ethics in the Clinical Curriculum
text_snippet: Integration of Social Science and Ethics in the Clinical Curriculum Introduction Social Sciences are an important part of the medical school curriculum, highlighted by the General Medical Council’s Outcomes for Graduates. However, the integration of social science in the clinical curriculum can be challenging. We sought to review the integration of social science in the clinical curriculum of a Scottish Medical School to identify gaps and opportunities. Methods We carried out an audit of the integration of key topics in the clinical curriculum. Fifteen key topics, taught under the title of ‘Social and Ethical Aspects of Medicine’ (‘SEAM’) were identified. All content for the clinical curriculum available on the virtual learning environment was reviewed and information extracted: what was taught, in what years, the teaching modality, and the type and level of knowledge provided, based on Bloom’s taxonomy. Results This review was carried out over January–July 2023 on the Edinburgh Medical School Year 4–6 MBChB Clinical Curriculum. In total, 449 SEAM learning experiences were identified (Year 4 n = 165; Year 5 n = 143; Year 6 n = 141). All SEAM topics introduced in the early years were covered at least once over years 4–6. title: Guided Drawing as a Learning Strategy in Head & Neck Embryology
text_snippet: Guided Drawing as a Learning Strategy in Head & Neck Embryology Introduction/Background Drawing-to-learn strategies may improve understanding of complex anatomical content, but evidence in anatomy, particularly embryology, is limited. Methods Incoming second-year medical students were randomized to a guided drawing group or a viewing-only group during a voluntary summer embryology exercise. Both groups completed identical asynchronous modules: the drawing group followed step-by-step tutorials, while the control group viewed completed illustrations. Knowledge was assessed using a 10-item pretest, immediate post-test, and delayed post-test. Mann-Whitney U tests and effect sizes were calculated. Results/Findings Thirty-two students completed the pre-test; 21 completed the immediate post-test; 16 completed the delayed post-test. Both groups improved immediately. The drawing group demonstrated larger learning gains (moderate effect), though differences were not statistically significant. At delayed testing, scores declined in both groups, but the drawing group showed smaller knowledge loss (moderate effect). title: What is the ideal duration of a medical lecture? A systematic review of factors influencing medical student learning and engagement.
text_snippet: What is the ideal duration of a medical lecture? A systematic review of factors influencing medical student learning and engagement. Introduction Lectures remain a central component of undergraduate medical education worldwide. However, concerns have emerged that traditional lecture durations may not align with contemporary understanding of attention, cognitive load and student engagement. 1–4 Despite ongoing debate, there is no clear consensus on the optimal length of a medical lecture. This systematic review aimed to synthesise existing literature examining lecture duration and its relationship with medical student concentration, engagement and learning outcomes. 5 Methods This systematic review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. Comprehensive searches were performed across Medline, Embase and ERIC without language or date restrictions. After duplicate removal, 6508 titles and abstracts were screened. Full texts were assessed against predefined inclusion criteria and five studies met eligibility requirements. 7–11 Forward and backward citation tracking was also undertaken to ensure comprehensive coverage. title: Learning-by-Concordance in Dermatology: A Continuing Medical Education Model for Family Physicians
text_snippet: Learning-by-Concordance in Dermatology: A Continuing Medical Education Model for Family Physicians Introduction Dermatologic conditions are frequently encountered in primary care, yet family physicians often lack confidence and up-to-date knowledge in dermatology. Traditional continuing medical education (CME) methods struggle to meet the practical needs of busy clinicians. We aim to describe the development, implementation, and impact of an innovative online dermatology CME program based on Learning-by-Concordance (LbC) for family physicians in Quebec. Methods Eight online modules were created using LbC methodology, presenting clinical vignettes with expert feedback to stimulate clinical reasoning. Modules were accessed asynchronously. Participant feedback was collected through post-module surveys. Results 322 primary care physicians across Quebec completed at least one module. Learners reported increased knowledge, improved diagnostic reasoning, and high satisfaction with the format. Participants noted greater diagnostic confidence and described concrete changes in their patient management. 89% found the content applicable to their practice, and 84% recommended the program for broader use. Discussion This study supports the effectiveness of LbC as a CME format in dermatology.

title: Is your curriculum GenAI-proof? A method for GenAI impact assessment and a case study
text_snippet: Is your curriculum GenAI-proof? A method for GenAI impact assessment and a case study Background Generative AI (GenAI) can complete tasks that previously could only be performed successfully by humans. Although GenAI provides many opportunities, it also poses risks such as invalid assessments and irrelevant learning outcomes. This article presents a broadly applicable method to (1) determine current assessment validity, (2) assess which learning outcomes are impacted by student GenAI use and (3) decide whether to alter assessment formats and/or learning outcomes. This is exemplified by a case-study on our Medical Informatics curriculum. We developed a five-step method to evaluate and address the impact of GenAI. Together with the respective lecturers, all assessments in the courses comprising a curriculum are analysed and subsequently adapted to address the impact of GenAI usage. Results 57% (55/96) of assessments, especially for courses involving writing and programming, were at risk of reduced validity and relevance. GenAI impact on assessment validity was closer related to the content and structure of assessments than to their complexity according to Bloom’s taxonomy. title: Designing Faculty Development for AI Skill Building in Health Professions Education: Applied Insights from a Longitudinal Program
text_snippet: Designing Faculty Development for AI Skill Building in Health Professions Education: Applied Insights from a Longitudinal Program AI skill development is essential in health professions education (HPE), yet this type of faculty development is complex to design and implement. While competency frameworks and AI education programs are emerging, many faculty developers are themselves still building AI literacy and confidence, and practical guidance for how to design a faculty development program on AI that is accessible, skill-oriented, and responsive to rapid technological change remains limited. Although webinars and workshops can only do so much, a well-planned faculty development program can provide a great introduction to AI, alleviate fears, and inspire participants to keep growing and learning. Drawing on our experience designing and hosting the AAMC GEA AI Skill-Building Webinar Series and the current literature in AI, this article offers twelve practical tips for faculty developers who are creating AI-focused learning opportunities for everyone involved in HPE. These tips will help readers create robust AI skill-building sessions that move participants beyond awareness of AI and shift their perspectives toward applied, reflective, and responsible use of AI in HPE.

title: Stronger Together: A Longitudinal Follow-Up Study of Psychiatric Educators Participating in an International Faculty Development Program
text_snippet: Stronger Together: A Longitudinal Follow-Up Study of Psychiatric Educators Participating in an International Faculty Development Program Objective Faculty development is an important factor in professional identity formation for health profession educators. The Association for Academic Psychiatry’s Master Educator Program is a faculty development program for psychiatric educators. We explored changes in participants’ academic contributions and perceived benefits 1–6 years after program participation. Methods We conducted a prospective, longitudinal study of participants who attended at least one Master Educator session from September 2018 to September 2023. Survey 1 (baseline, administered before each session) and Survey 2 (follow-up, conducted once in 2024) captured demographics, academic productivity, leadership roles, and perceived program impact. Pre- to post-group comparisons and within-participant changes were assessed using McNemar’s and Stuart-Maxwell tests. Open-ended comments were analyzed qualitatively. Results Survey 1 was distributed to 220 participants, receiving responses from 150 unique individuals (68.2% response rate). Of those, 52 (34.7%) also completed Survey 2. title: Evaluating the Impact of Entrustable Professional Activity Based Medical Student Teaching and Logbook Usage on Competence and Confidence in Peripheral Intravenous Cannulation
text_snippet: Evaluating the Impact of Entrustable Professional Activity Based Medical Student Teaching and Logbook Usage on Competence and Confidence in Peripheral Intravenous Cannulation Introduction Entrustable Professional Activities (EPAs) are specific and measurable units of clinical practice used in competency-based training. Learners demonstrate skills to assessors who assign supervision levels for future practice. This study evaluated the impact of EPA-based assessment and logbook use on medical student performance and confidence in peripheral intravenous (IV) cannulation. Methods This multi-phase mixed methods study involved medical students attending a teaching course incorporating EPA-based teaching and assessment. Participants were divided into test and control groups. Self-assessed confidence scores and EPA levels were measured before and after the teaching course comparing logbook and non-logbook users. Thematic analysis of student and assessor feedback explored perceptions of EPA assessment and course effectiveness. title: Evaluating How Artificial Intelligence Tools Influence Educational Outcomes, Usage Patterns, and User Perceptions in Research Proposal Development: A Convergent Mixed Methods Study.
text_snippet: Evaluating How Artificial Intelligence Tools Influence Educational Outcomes, Usage Patterns, and User Perceptions in Research Proposal Development: A Convergent Mixed Methods Study. Abstract Background Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into higher education, including medical education, particularly for research training and academic writing. Research methodology and biostatistics courses are often perceived as challenging, with students reporting difficulty structuring research proposals, interpreting statistical concepts, and applying theoretical knowledge to research practice. This study aimed to assess the perceived benefits, challenges, ethical considerations, and implementation needs associated with a customized AI tool for research proposal writing among fourth-year medical students enrolled in a Research Methodology and Biostatistics course. Methods A convergent mixed-methods design was used. A customized ChatGPT-based Research Proposal Smart Tool (RPST-GPT) was developed and provided to students to support proposal development.
